item.research_question: How do strong homogeneous and gradient magnetic fields affect the nucleation behavior, undercooling, and recalescence of a highly undercooled Co76Sn24 near-eutectic alloy?
item.material_system: Co76Sn24 (at. %) near-eutectic alloy with B2O3 glass slag flux
item.processing_route: Cold crucible levitation melting to prepare ingots, followed by glass slag fluxing in a quartz tube crucible inside a 12 T superconducting magnet; heating/cooling rates controlled by furnace; homogeneous field (12 T) and gradient field (93 T/m) applied during cooling
item.test_conditions: Temperature range up to 1437 K; homogeneous magnetic field of 12 T; gradient magnetic field of 93 T/m (field intensity at sample position 6.23 T); cyclic heating; undercooling measured via two-color pyrometer (50 Hz); magnetic force monitored via electronic balance
key_findings: Mean undercooling without magnetic field is 246 K, remaining unchanged at 245 K under 12 T homogeneous field.
Mean undercooling decreases to 232 K under a 93 T/m gradient magnetic field (a reduction of 14 K).
Recalescence extent (ΔT R-N) decreases from 177 K (0 T) to 134 K (12 T homogeneous field) in the first 10 cycles.
Recalescence extent increases from 177 K (0 T) to 194 K under 93 T/m gradient magnetic field.
Calculated magnetic Gibbs free energy (ΔG M) is 28 J/mol, only ~1% of the chemical Gibbs free energy (ΔH f = 13.027 kJ/mol).
Volume fraction of anomalous eutectics formed during recalescence is 95.8% (0 T), 96.4% (12 T), and 99.5% (gradient field).
The undercooled melt remains in a paramagnetic state down to the nucleation temperature (1152 K).
The magnetic force exerted on the sample in the gradient field is approximately 17 times the sample's weight.
item.mechanism: The magnetic field has a negligible effect on nucleation thermodynamics because the magnetic Gibbs free energy is only ~1% of the chemical driving force. In homogeneous fields, the unchanged undercooling is due to this weak thermodynamic effect, while the reduced recalescence is attributed to magnetic-field-induced defects (dislocations, vacancies) storing energy. In gradient fields, the paramagnetic melt experiences a strong downward compressive force that alters the sample shape, disrupts the equilibrium with the glass slag, and weakens the slag's purifying effect, thereby reducing undercooling; the increased recalescence is due to a higher volume fraction of solidification during the rapid release of latent heat.
item.limitations: The authors state it is not easy to undercool the Co-Sn alloy below its liquid Curie temperature with the present technique, which limits the observation of magnetic contributions to nucleation temperature. The effect of magnetic field on the heating/cooling kinetics was found to be very limited.
quotes: The mean undercooling of the undercooled melt is not altered by homogeneous magnetic field but depressed by gradient magnetic field.
The application of magnetic field just add about 1% of the total energy of the system, so that its effect on the thermodynamics of nucleation is very weak.
The gradient magnetic field will reduce the mean undercooling which is attributed to the magnetic force exerted on the undercooled liquid which can break the purifying and nucleation condition.

Processing: Cold crucible levitation melting to prepare ingots, followed by glass slag fluxing in a quartz tube crucible inside a 12 T superconducting magnet; heating/cooling rates controlled by furnace; homogeneous field (12 T) and gradient field (93 T/m) applied during cooling. Test conditions: Temperature range up to 1437 K; homogeneous magnetic field of 12 T; gradient magnetic field of 93 T/m (field intensity at sample position 6.23 T); cyclic heating; undercooling measured via two-color pyrometer (50 Hz); magnetic force monitored via electronic balance.
